claim: 202 iPSC lines derived from 151 donors were analyzed with integrated transcriptome and genomic sequence data from the same lines.
source: Here, we present the first comprehensive proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC), a key cell type for disease modelling, analysing 202 iPSC lines derived from 151 donors, with integrated transcriptome and genomic sequence data from the same lines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of iPSC lines and donors analyzed in the study.

claim: 654 protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) were identified in iPSCs.
source: We identified 654 protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) in iPSCs, including disease-linked variants in protein-coding sequences and variants with trans regulatory effects.
evidence: The abstract explicitly reports the number of pQTLs identified.

claim: Some pQTLs are linked to GWAS variants that cannot be detected at the mRNA level.
source: These include pQTL linked to GWAS variants that cannot be detected at the mRNA level, highlighting the utility of dissecting pQTL at peptide level resolution.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that some pQTLs linked to GWAS variants are not detectable at mRNA level.

claim: 255,015 distinct peptide sequences were identified, corresponding to 16,773 protein groups with median sequence coverage of 46%.
source: Collectively, we identified 255,015 distinct (unmodified) peptide sequences, corresponding to 16,773 protein groups (groups of protein isoforms with no discriminating peptides; hereon denoted proteins) with median sequence coverage of 46%.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of peptides and protein groups identified.

claim: 11,140 recurrently detected proteins were identified, corresponding to 10,198 genes.
source: We identified 11,140 recurrently detected proteins, corresponding to 10,198 genes (detected in at least 30 lines; Materials and methods) and RNA expression for 12,363 protein-coding genes (population average TPM >1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the number of recurrently detected proteins and corresponding genes.

claim: 9013 protein coding genes were detected both at the RNA and protein levels.
source: Out of these, 9013 protein coding genes were detected both at the RNA and protein levels (Figure 1—source datas 2 and 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes detected at both RNA and protein levels.

claim: The iPSC proteome was most similar to foetal and reproductive organs.
source: When overlaying our data with the Human Proteome Map (Kim et al., 2014), the iPSC proteome was most similar to foetal and reproductive organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which is consistent with the expected expression of pluripotency markers in these tissues (Kerr et al., 2008a; Kerr et al., 2008b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the similarity of iPSC proteome to foetal and reproductive organs, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No systematic expression differences were identified between healthy donors and disease-bearing donors in the iPSC state.
source: We also assessed differences between healthy donors and disease-bearing donors, identifying no systematic expression differences in the iPSC state (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states that no systematic differences were found between healthy and disease-bearing donors.

claim: The fraction of variance explained by biological factors was lower for protein levels compared to RNA variation.
source: Overall, the fraction of variance explained by biological factors was lower for protein levels, compared to RNA variation, which points to higher assay noise and/or stochastic variability of protein abundance.
evidence: The Results section explicitly compares variance explained at protein vs RNA levels.

claim: Donor genome is the most relevant factor explaining protein expression variation, followed by culture medium.
source: Consistent with previous results using RNA data (Kilpinen et al., 2017), we identified donor genome (i.e. DNA sequence variation) as the most relevant factor, followed by culture medium (Figure 1b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies donor genome as the most relevant factor, supported by Figure 1b.

claim: Significant donor effects remained after accounting for RNA variability.
source: Critically, however, significant donor effects remained after accounting for RNA variability (Figure 1b,d; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states that donor effects persist after adjusting for RNA.

claim: Genetic differences between individual donors and experimental differences between culture conditions play an important role in causing the observed variation in proteome expression between the iPSC lines.
source: This indicates that (i) genetic differences between individual donors and experimental differences between culture conditions play an important role in causing the observed variation in proteome expression between the iPSC lines and (ii) post-transcriptional mechanisms also contribute to these effects.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the role of genetic and experimental differences.

claim: Post-transcriptional mechanisms contribute to protein expression variation.
source: This indicates that (i) genetic differences between individual donors and experimental differences between culture conditions play an important role in causing the observed variation in proteome expression between the iPSC lines and (ii) post-transcriptional mechanisms also contribute to these effects.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states that post-transcriptional mechanisms contribute to effects.

claim: 88 proteins showed a strong (>20%) gender-related effect on expression.
source: There was also a strong (i.e. >20%) gender-related effect on the expression of a subset of 88 proteins (Figure 1b), which are enriched for proteins encoded on the X chromosome (Odds ratio = 24.8, PV = 3×10−32, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of proteins with gender-related effects.

claim: Proteins showing strong gender-related effects are enriched for proteins encoded on the X chromosome (Odds ratio = 24.8, PV = 3×10−32).
source: There was also a strong (i.e. >20%) gender-related effect on the expression of a subset of 88 proteins (Figure 1b), which are enriched for proteins encoded on the X chromosome (Odds ratio = 24.8, PV = 3×10−32, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the enrichment statistics.

claim: 1374 genes showed changes in protein or RNA levels correlated with XCI status (FDR < 10%).
source: This identified 1374 genes for which either protein, or RNA levels, or both, showed changes correlated with XCI status (Figure 1c, FDR < 10%; Figure 1—source data 5).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes affected by XCI status.

claim: XCI status preferentially impacts catabolic processes and mitochondria at the protein level, while this was not observed at the RNA level.
source: Further analysis indicated that XCI status preferentially impacts catabolic processes and mitochondria at the protein level, while this was not observed at the RNA level (Gene Ontology; Materials and methods; Figure 1c; Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the differential impact of XCI status at protein vs RNA levels.

claim: 654 genes have at least one cis pQTL (FDR < 10%).
source: Across all autosomal genes, we report 654 genes with at least one cis pQTL and 3487 genes with a cis eQTL (FDR < 10% for both eQTL and pQTL mapping; lead variants only; Figure 2a; Figure 2—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with cis pQTLs.

claim: 3487 genes have a cis eQTL (FDR < 10%).
source: Across all autosomal genes, we report 654 genes with at least one cis pQTL and 3487 genes with a cis eQTL (FDR < 10% for both eQTL and pQTL mapping; lead variants only; Figure 2a; Figure 2—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with cis eQTLs.

claim: 273 genes had shared pQTL and eQTL with identical or correlated lead variants.
source: Among these, 273 genes were shared and had identical or correlated lead variants, whereas 82 genes showed evidence for an eQTL and pQTL with independent lead variants (LD-based criterion, r2 <0.1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with shared QTLs.

claim: 82 genes showed evidence for an eQTL and pQTL with independent lead variants (r2 <0.1).
source: Among these, 273 genes were shared and had identical or correlated lead variants, whereas 82 genes showed evidence for an eQTL and pQTL with independent lead variants (LD-based criterion, r2 <0.1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with independent QTLs.

claim: Genes with substantial donor components (>20%) were enriched for significant cis pQTL (Odds ratio = 4.2).
source: Genes with substantial donor components, as identified based on the variance component analysis (>20%; Figure 1b), were enriched for significant cis pQTL (215 genes out of 962; Odds ratio = 4.2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the enrichment of pQTLs in genes with substantial donor components.

claim: 473 pQTLs (72%) had replicated eQTL effects.
source: This identified 473 pQTLs (72%) with replicated eQTL effects.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number and percentage of pQTLs with replicated eQTL effects.

claim: 893 eQTLs (26%) had replicated protein effects.
source: Conversely, 893 eQTLs (26%) had replicated protein effects, with globally concordant effect size directions and distance from gene boundaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number and percentage of eQTLs with replicated protein effects.

claim: eQTL effect size is a strong predictor for protein replication, with larger effects being associated with increased replication rates.
source: We identified the eQTL effect size as a strong predictor for protein replication, with larger effects being associated with increased replication rates (Figure 2c).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies eQTL effect size as a predictor of protein replication.

claim: 136 (of 654) pQTL signals tag a known GWAS variant (r2 >0.8).
source: Specifically, we probed for QTLs that tag GWAS variants contained in the GWAS catalogue (MacArthur et al., 2017) (i.e. are in LD r2 >0.8), identifying 136 (of 654) pQTL signals that tag a known GWAS variant (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of pQTLs that tag GWAS variants.

claim: 49 pQTLs showed evidence of co-localisation with GWAS signals (cumulative co-localisation probability greater than 0.1).
source: In addition, we assessed the statistical evidence for co-localisation of pQTL and GWAS signals for 51 studies for which full summary statistics were obtained (using eCAVIAR Hormozdiari et al., 2016; Materials and methods; Figure 2—source data 1), yielding 49 pQTLs with evidence of co-localisation (i.e cumulative co-localisation probability greater than 0.1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of pQTLs with co-localisation evidence.

claim: rs7872034 is a pQTL for SMC2 with co-localisation evidence for serous invasive ovarian cancer (Phelan et al., 2017).
source: Among these, examples of pQTLs with corresponding effects at the RNA level include the variant rs7872034, a pQTL for SMC2 with co-localisation evidence for serous invasive ovarian cancer (Phelan et al., 2017), and the variant rs11752813, a pQTL for PEX6 and in LD with Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers risk variant rs1129187 (Jun et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies rs7872034 as a pQTL for SMC2 with GWAS co-localisation.

claim: rs11752813 is a pQTL for PEX6 and in LD with Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers risk variant rs1129187 (Jun et al., 2016).
source: Among these, examples of pQTLs with corresponding effects at the RNA level include the variant rs7872034, a pQTL for SMC2 with co-localisation evidence for serous invasive ovarian cancer (Phelan et al., 2017), and the variant rs11752813, a pQTL for PEX6 and in LD with Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers risk variant rs1129187 (Jun et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies rs11752813 as a pQTL for PEX6 linked to Alzheimer's disease risk.

claim: 33 pQTLs linked to GWAS variants had no replicated effect at the RNA level, suggesting protein-specific regulation.
source: Notably, for 33 pQTLs linked to GWAS variants, either via co-localisation or LD tagging, no replicated effect was identified at the RNA level, suggesting protein-specific regulation (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of pQTLs with protein-specific regulation.

claim: rs11601507 has no RNA effects, and is associated with TRIM5 protein abundance and with coronary artery disease risk (van der Harst and Verweij, 2018).
source: For example, rs11601507 has no RNA effects, and is associated with TRIM5 protein abundance and with coronary artery disease risk (van der Harst and Verweij, 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies rs11601507 as a protein-specific pQTL associated with disease risk.

claim: 3810 genes have a transcript QTL (tQTL).
source: cis QTL mapping of 33,050 reference transcript isoforms (Zerbino et al., 2018) (quantified using Salmon Patro et al., 2017; Materials and methods) and 119,747 peptides identified 3810 genes with a transcript QTL (tQTL) and 566 genes with a peptide QTL (pepQTL), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with transcript QTLs.

claim: 566 genes have a peptide QTL (pepQTL).
source: cis QTL mapping of 33,050 reference transcript isoforms (Zerbino et al., 2018) (quantified using Salmon Patro et al., 2017; Materials and methods) and 119,747 peptides identified 3810 genes with a transcript QTL (tQTL) and 566 genes with a peptide QTL (pepQTL), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of genes with peptide QTLs.

claim: For 48 eQTLs without replicated pQTL effect, the eQTL variant was exclusively associated with abundance changes of non-coding transcript isoforms (nominal PV <0.01).
source: Transcript-level QTL mapping could explain the lack of protein effects for a small fraction of the 2594 eQTL without a replicated pQTL effect (Figure 2a). For 48 of these, the eQTL variant was identified as exclusively associated with abundance changes of non-coding transcript isoforms (nominal PV <0.01), which explains the absence of protein effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of eQTLs affecting non-coding isoforms.

claim: Among 181 pQTLs without eQTL replication, 61 had nominally significant transcript QTLs (PV <0.01).
source: Among 181 pQTLs without eQTL replication (Figure 2a), 61 had nominally significant transcript QTLs (PV <0.01; Figure 3a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of pQTLs with transcript QTL effects.

claim: For 12 pQTLs without eQTL replication, genetic effects with opposite directions on coding and non-coding transcript isoforms were observed.
source: For 12 of these, including a pQTL for MMAB (Figure 3b), we observed genetic effects with opposite directions on coding and non-coding transcript isoforms, which explains the lack of genetic effects when considering gene-level RNA abundance.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of pQTLs with opposite directional effects on isoforms.

claim: 24 pQTL lead variants without replication at eQTL or transcript QTL levels are inframe variants.
source: When classifying the corresponding lead pQTL variants based on their predicted functional effect, we identified 24 inframe variants, a striking enrichment compared to pQTL with replicated RNA effects (3.8-fold enrichment; PV = 4×10−5, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3c and d).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of inframe variants among RNA-independent pQTLs.

claim: RNA-independent pQTLs show a 3.8-fold enrichment for inframe variants (PV = 4×10−5).
source: When classifying the corresponding lead pQTL variants based on their predicted functional effect, we identified 24 inframe variants, a striking enrichment compared to pQTL with replicated RNA effects (3.8-fold enrichment; PV = 4×10−5, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3c and d).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the enrichment statistics for inframe variants.

claim: For 11 of the 24 RNA-independent pQTLs, no evidence of eQTL nominal significance was found in any of the 48 GTEx tissues (PV <0.01/48).
source: We assessed whether the 24 pQTL have effects at the RNA level (eQTL) in other cell types, and for 11 of these pQTL we did not find evidence of eQTL nominal significance in any of the 48 GTEx (PV <0.01/48; Battle et al., 2017; Figure 1—source data 1), which further points to RNA-independent mechanisms.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the lack of eQTL evidence in GTEx for 11 pQTLs.

claim: 10 of the 24 RNA-independent pQTLs that tag inframe variants have predicted deleterious effects (SIFT score <0.05).
source: We estimated whether a variant is likely to be deleterious to protein function using SIFT scores, which capture evolutionary conservation and amino acid similarity (Ng and Henikoff, 2003). This revealed a clear enrichment of the 24 RNA-independent pQTL that tag inframe variants, 10 of which have predicted deleterious effects (SIFT score <0.05), compared to four among all other pQTL (Odds ratio = 27.5, PV = 3.8×10−8, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of deleterious variants among RNA-independent pQTLs.

claim: RNA-independent pQTLs with inframe variants show enrichment for deleterious effects (Odds ratio = 27.5, PV = 3.8×10−8).
source: This revealed a clear enrichment of the 24 RNA-independent pQTL that tag inframe variants, 10 of which have predicted deleterious effects (SIFT score <0.05), compared to four among all other pQTL (Odds ratio = 27.5, PV = 3.8×10−8, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the enrichment statistics for deleterious effects.

claim: The variant rs1051061 in VRK2 lies in a conserved sequence in the kinase domain, proximal to the proton acceptor residue, likely impacting kinase activity.
source: For example, the variant rs1051061 in VRK2 lies in a conserved sequence in the kinase domain, proximal to the proton acceptor residue, likely impacting kinase activity (Figure 3c).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the location and predicted impact of rs1051061.

claim: The variant rs1051061 has been identified as GWAS risk variant for schizophrenia (Yu et al., 2017) (OR 1.17).
source: The identical variant has been identified as GWAS risk variant for schizophrenia (Yu et al., 2017) (OR 1.17), with the risk allele being associated with decreased protein abundance.
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies rs1051061 as a schizophrenia risk variant.

claim: The risk allele of rs1051061 is associated with decreased VRK2 protein abundance.
source: The identical variant has been identified as GWAS risk variant for schizophrenia (Yu et al., 2017) (OR 1.17), with the risk allele being associated with decreased protein abundance.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the association between the risk allele and decreased protein abundance.

claim: 51 cis-pQTL lead variants have trans effects on a total of 68 proteins (FDR < 10%).
source: We mapped proteome-wide trans pQTL, considering 654 cis pQTL variants. This identified 51 cis-pQTL lead variants with trans effects on a total of 68 proteins (FDR < 10%; Figure 4—source data 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the number of cis-pQTL variants with trans effects.

claim: Pairs of proteins with shared genetic regulation were strongly enriched for known protein-protein interactions (Odds ratio = 9.1, PV = 1.5×10−10).
source: The detected pairs of proteins with shared genetic regulation were strongly enriched for known protein-protein interactions (CORUM Ruepp et al., 2010, IntAct Orchard et al., 2014, StringDB Szklarczyk et al., 2017; Odds ratio = 9.1, PV = 1.5×10−10, Fisher's exact test; Figure 4b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the enrichment of protein-protein interactions among trans pQTLs.

claim: The cis and trans effects had similar effect directions and effect sizes, consistent with genetic effects mediated via stabilising protein-protein interactions.
source: The cis and trans effects had similar effect directions and effect sizes, consistent with genetic effects mediated via stabilising protein-protein interactions (Figure 4c).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the similarity of effect directions and sizes.

claim: The variant rs1129187 is associated in cis with an increase in both PEX6 RNA and protein abundance.
source: As noted above, the underlying pQTL variant rs1129187 is associated in cis with an increase in both PEX6 RNA and protein abundance (Figure 2b) and is a known risk variant for Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers (Jun et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the cis association of rs1129187 with PEX6.

claim: The variant rs1129187 is a known risk variant for Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers (Jun et al., 2016).
source: As noted above, the underlying pQTL variant rs1129187 is associated in cis with an increase in both PEX6 RNA and protein abundance (Figure 2b) and is a known risk variant for Alzheimer's disease in APOE e4+ carriers (Jun et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies rs1129187 as an Alzheimer's disease risk variant.

claim: The cis pQTL rs1129187 induces downstream associations on the remaining complex subunits, PEX26 and PEX1.
source: This cis pQTL in turn induces downstream associations on the remaining complex subunits, PEX26 and PEX1 (Figure 4e), suggesting that PEX6 acts as a limiting subunit of this complex in iPSCs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the trans effects on PEX26 and PEX1.

claim: PEX6 acts as a limiting subunit of the PEX26-PEX6-PEX1 complex in iPSCs.
source: This cis pQTL in turn induces downstream associations on the remaining complex subunits, PEX26 and PEX1 (Figure 4e), suggesting that PEX6 acts as a limiting subunit of this complex in iPSCs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly suggests PEX6 as a limiting subunit.

claim: There is prior evidence for an implication of peroxisomal function in the development of Alzheimer's disease and in other neurodegenerative processes (Lizard et al., 2012; Berger et al., 2016).
source: Notably, there is prior evidence for an implication of peroxisomal function in the development of Alzheimer's disease and in other neurodegenerative processes (Lizard et al., 2012; Berger et al., 2016), providing further support for this hypothesis.
evidence: The Results section explicitly cites prior evidence for peroxisomal function in Alzheimer's disease.

claim: This study provides the most detailed population-level analysis of parallel RNA/protein profiles in human cells.
source: Beyond the relevance for iPS cell biology, this study, to our knowledge, provides the most detailed population-level analysis of parallel RNA/protein profiles in human cells.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly claims this is the most detailed population-level analysis.

claim: More than 600 cis protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) were mapped.
source: By quantifying genome-wide protein and transcript expression variation across more than 200 human iPSC lines, we identified both genetic and non-genetic mechanisms that underlie variation in both protein and RNA levels. We have mapped more than 600 cis protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) and analysed how these relate to cis eQTLs, how they impact other proteins in trans, and how pQTLs link to human disease variants.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states that more than 600 cis pQTLs were mapped.

claim: The variance component analysis explained a lower overall fraction of variance in the protein data compared to RNA variation.
source: The variance component analysis explained a lower overall fraction of variance in the protein data compared to RNA variation, which likely reflects larger technical effects and/or stochasticity in protein expression levels.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states that variance explained is lower for protein data.

claim: Donor-specific genetic factors are a major contributor to the differences in protein expression detected across the iPSC lines.
source: Among the explainable fraction of variance, donor-specific genetic factors are a major contributor to the differences in protein expression detected across the iPSC lines.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly identifies donor-specific genetic factors as major contributors.

claim: Protein expression variation across iPS cells reflects genetic diversity in the human population.
source: The corollary is that protein expression variation across iPS cells reflects genetic diversity in the human population.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states that protein variation reflects genetic diversity.

claim: There were substantially fewer pQTLs than eQTLs.
source: Globally, there were substantially fewer pQTLs than eQTLs, and while most pQTLs had effects of the same direction at eQTL, only 30% of eQTLs are nominally significant at the protein level.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly compares the number of pQTLs and eQTLs.

claim: Only 30% of eQTLs are nominally significant at the protein level.
source: Globally, there were substantially fewer pQTLs than eQTLs, and while most pQTLs had effects of the same direction at eQTL, only 30% of eQTLs are nominally significant at the protein level.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the percentage of eQTLs significant at protein level.

claim: Many eQTLs may reflect variation in RNA abundance that does not cause significant changes in steady state protein levels.
source: Instead, many eQTLs may reflect variation in RNA abundance that does not cause significant changes in steady state protein levels.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly suggests that many eQTLs do not affect protein levels.

claim: Isoform-resolution protein and RNA phenotypes are indispensable to fully understand the propagation of genetic effects to proteins.
source: By the systematic comparison of matched protein and RNA data, including detailed analysis of separate isoforms, we demonstrated that in order to fully understand the propagation of genetic effects to proteins, isoform-resolution protein and RNA phenotypes are indispensable.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the importance of isoform-resolution analysis.

claim: pQTLs for which no corresponding changes in transcript levels were detected are enriched in deleterious missense variants.
source: We showed that the pQTLs for which no corresponding changes in transcript levels were detected, are enriched in deleterious missense variants.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the enrichment of deleterious missense variants in RNA-independent pQTLs.

claim: The phenotypic effects of deleterious missense variants may be exerted through protein abundance changes.
source: This result suggests that the phenotypic effects of such variations may be exerted through protein abundance changes.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly suggests that deleterious variants act through protein abundance changes.

claim: This study presents the first comprehensive map of pQTLs at peptide resolution, considering a total of 119,747 peptides from 8543 proteins for genetic analysis.
source: Our study presents the first comprehensive map of pQTLs at peptide resolution, considering a total of 119,747 peptides from 8543 proteins for genetic analysis.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly claims this is the first comprehensive peptide-resolution pQTL map.

claim: 566 peptide QTL were identified.
source: This identified 566 peptide QTL, several of which were not detectable when considering whole protein expression levels, as illustrated with the variant rs12795503, pepQTL for gene CTTN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly reports the number of peptide QTLs identified.

claim: Protein-protein interactions can propagate genetic effects in human populations.
source: Our data highlight the ability of protein-protein interactions to propagate genetic effects in human populations.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states that protein-protein interactions propagate genetic effects.

claim: cis eQTLs affecting the levels of rate-limiting subunits should have effects in trans on the abundance of the whole complex.
source: A long-standing hypothesis has been that certain protein complexes may have a rate-limiting subunit that determines complex abundance, with any excess subunits produced being rapidly degraded (e.g. because of exposure of hydrophobic residues). This implies that cis eQTLs affecting the levels of rate-limiting subunits should also have effects in trans on the abundance of the whole complex, and on most, if not all, subunits therein.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes the hypothesis about rate-limiting subunits.

claim: This study provides the first example that trans genetic effects mediated by protein interactions act through common genetic variants in untransformed human cells.
source: While trans genetic effects were previously reported to be mediated by protein interactions in high heterozygosity samples, that is outbred mice, (Chick et al., 2016) and for somatic aberrations in cancer cell lines (Gonçalves et al., 2017; Roumeliotis et al., 2017), to our knowledge, this study provides the first example that such effects act through common genetic variants in untransformed human cells.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly claims this is the first example in untransformed human cells.

claim: Direct analysis of human iPSCs can advance our understanding of the genetic regulation of protein expression and how this influences cell phenotypes and disease mechanisms.
source: This study provides important information showing how direct analysis of human iPSCs can advance our understanding of the genetic regulation of protein expression and how this influences cell phenotypes and disease mechanisms.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states the utility of iPSC analysis for understanding genetic regulation.

claim: All HipSci samples were collected from consented research volunteers recruited from the NIHR Cambridge BioResource.
source: As described in Kilpinen et al., 2017, all HipSci samples were collected from consented research volunteers recruited from the NIHR Cambridge BioResource, and iPSC were generated from fibroblasts by transduction with Sendai vectors.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the sample source.

claim: iPSC were generated from fibroblasts by transduction with Sendai vectors.
source: As described in Kilpinen et al., 2017, all HipSci samples were collected from consented research volunteers recruited from the NIHR Cambridge BioResource, and iPSC were generated from fibroblasts by transduction with Sendai vectors.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the iPSC generation method.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry was carried out in batches of 10 lines, using tandem mass tagging (TMT).
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry was carried out in batches of 10 lines, using tandem mass tagging (TMT, Thompson et al., 2003), with one common reference sample shared across batches (Brenes et al., 2018) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the mass spectrometry approach.

claim: One common reference sample was shared across TMT batches.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry was carried out in batches of 10 lines, using tandem mass tagging (TMT, Thompson et al., 2003), with one common reference sample shared across batches (Brenes et al., 2018) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the use of a common reference sample.

claim: TMT-ten plex was used to label ten IPSC lines and quantify them in parallel.
source: TMT-ten plex was used to label ten IPSC lines and quantify them in parallel.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the TMT-ten plex approach.

claim: 24 TMT-ten plex experiments were performed.
source: In total, 24 TMT-ten plex experiments were performed, where one IPSC line (HPSI0314i-bubh_3) was chosen as a reference cell line and was kept constant in all TMT batches.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states the number of TMT experiments.

claim: HPSI0314i-bubh_3 was chosen as a reference cell line and was kept constant in all TMT batches.
source: In total, 24 TMT-ten plex experiments were performed, where one IPSC line (HPSI0314i-bubh_3) was chosen as a reference cell line and was kept constant in all TMT batches.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly identifies the reference cell line.

claim: 6273 peptides that overlap polymorphisms were discarded from further analyses.
source: This resulted in 6273 peptides that overlap such polymorphisms, which were discarded from further analyses (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly reports the number of peptides discarded.

claim: 10 lines with fewer than 67,000 identified peptides were discarded.
source: We discarded 10 lines with fewer than 67,000 identified peptides (corresponding to 75% of the median number of peptides identified; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resulting in a proteomics dataset consisting of 207 lines, 202 of which had matched RNA-Seq data and hence were considered for further analysis.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly reports the number of lines discarded.

claim: 7 PEER factors were fit for protein and 13 PEER factors for RNA.
source: We fit 7 PEER factors for protein and 13 PEER factors for RNA, settings that were determined as the largest number of PEER factors that retain statistical independence of the inferred factors (R < 0.7; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly reports the number of PEER factors used.
